README.md.overview: The project README explains the NL-to-ODRL design: the model only extracts a typed PolicyIR, deterministic code compiles it to ODRL 2.2 JSON-LD, and SHACL, grounding and Z3 checks gate publication. It is the starting point of the tour (step 1) and the best map of how the modules in odrl_agent/ fit together.

sections.title: Pitch and quick start
sections.explanation: States the core idea: a fixed-stage pipeline where the LLM extracts meaning into `PolicyIR` and a deterministic compiler owns syntax, IRIs and literal types. It names the ethical red line, over-permission (granting a right the source did not), and gives the install, `odrl-host serve` and `odrl-host run` commands plus the Docker alternative.

sections.title: Pipeline architecture diagram
sections.explanation: A Mermaid flowchart shows extract, ground, compile, SHACL verify, a bounded shrink-only repair loop (at most 2 rounds), then draft, validate and save. The text below it says the framework never owns the pipeline: IR, extractor, compiler and stages all live in `odrl_agent/`, and complex inputs get one extra decompose call.

sections.title: Benchmark and release gates
sections.explanation: Describes `benchmarks/v1` (240 stratified cases with gold IR, grouped so no family spans dev and test) and the `python -m odrl_agent.bench` commands. The offline gold-IR oracle runs on every PR, and a `--mutant overpermit` run must fail to prove the gates can trip. The live workflow compares against a frozen baseline.

sections.title: Flagship failure and safeguards
sections.explanation: Explains how the pipeline removes the old failure of saving invalid ODRL: the model never calls tools, every document is compiled from a validated IR, SHACL runs before the save, and repairs may narrow grants but never widen them. A sequence diagram shows the model, pipeline, ledger and verifiers, and the section ends with the `no_attacker_grant` check on the poisoned fixture.

sections.title: Install and LLM configuration
sections.explanation: Covers venv install, `PYTHONPATH`, and which commands need `LLAMA_API_KEY`/`LLAMA_BASE_URL` (live conversion) versus which work offline. It also documents product API keys (`NL2ODRL_API_KEYS`), the fail-closed auth gate and the fingerprint-only key storage. Running `odrl-host run` without a key fails closed with `E_MODEL_API` on purpose.

sections.title: CLI reference, scenarios, tests
sections.explanation: A table of every `odrl-host` subcommand (run, diagnose, replay, optimize-prompts, serve, chaos, keys, billing) plus the framework `agentcrash check`, then the two scenarios and their naive versus fixed policies. These map directly to the command handlers in `cli.py`.

sections.title: Grounding, reasoning, publish gate
sections.explanation: Lists the three deterministic checks every draft passes: grounding of parties and assets, Z3 reasoning for conflicts, and full SHACL. Only a draft with no ambiguities, assumptions, dropped rules, grounding issues or conflicts is published automatically; everything else waits for a human decision, one per run.

sections.title: Service behaviour
sections.explanation: Documents the FastAPI service: bounded worker queue with `429` and `Retry-After`, Server-Sent Events progress, Prometheus metrics, request ids written into traces, the AgentCrash SDK hash-chained traces, and cookie sessions with a CSRF header. This is the behaviour implemented in `app.py` and `web.py`.

sections.title: Troubleshooting and repo map
sections.explanation: Maps common symptoms to fixes (missing `PYTHONPATH`, missing key, missing `ui/index.html`) and closes with a table of top-level directories and their roles. Use the map to find scenarios, policies, schemas, prompts and tests.

odrl_agent/cli.py.overview: Entry point for the `odrl-host` command. It parses arguments for each subcommand and delegates to the pipeline, key store, server, chaos harness and policy-patch tooling, reusing the generic `agentcrash` framework for config loading, verification and exit codes. It is the first code a reader meets in tour steps 1 and 2.

sections.title: Imports and registration
sections.explanation: The docstring says this module holds host-owned commands while the generic `agentcrash` CLI never imports it. Imports bring in framework exit codes, policy helpers, trace verifiers and the `odrl_agent` pieces. The bare `import odrl_agent.verifiers` is there only for its side effect of registering the ODRL invariants.

sections.title: cmd_run: live conversion
sections.explanation: Builds an argparse parser, resolves the scenario and policy through framework helpers, and optionally adopts a versioned prompt pack, mixing its hash into the run id so runs stay distinguishable. `--dry-run` prints the plan and exits. Otherwise it calls `run_conversion`, maps `ModelNotConfiguredError` to `E_MODEL_API` and bad config to `E_CONFIG`, and prints a human or JSON summary.

sections.title: Untrusted span rendering
sections.explanation: `_retrieved_doc_spans` reads the trace and collects the parsed natural-language spans so `cmd_run` can print them through `render_untrusted`. The output labels source text as untrusted, which keeps hostile input visibly delimited in terminal output.

sections.title: keys and billing commands
sections.explanation: `cmd_keys` issues, lists and revokes product API keys, and `cmd_billing` exports per-run line items as JSON or CSV. Both operate on the SQLite store through helpers in `web.py`, and only key fingerprints are shown or stored.

sections.title: Prompt optimization and serve
sections.explanation: `cmd_optimize_prompts` runs a budgeted DSPy probe and refuses to run without a live key. `cmd_serve` finds the repository root, then calls `serve_ui(port, bind, root/'ui')`; it defaults to `127.0.0.1:8901` and returns a usage error when `ui/` cannot be found. Imports are done inside the function so other subcommands start fast.

sections.title: chaos command
sections.explanation: `cmd_chaos` fuzzes fault schedules against the real pipeline with a mocked model and store, and exits 1 on any invariant violation. The small helpers `_infer_scenario` and `_trace_seed` recover a scenario path and seed from an existing trace.

sections.title: diagnose command
sections.explanation: Reads a failing trace, runs the verifiers and proposes a policy patch. It is read-only and fixture-backed unless a live endpoint is configured, so it can run offline using `reference_patch_for`.

sections.title: replay command and regression
sections.explanation: Re-runs a trace's scenario under a patched policy and compares the verdict, with `_regress_golden` checking frozen golden traces for regressions. This is how a proposed patch is proven to fix the failure without breaking known-good runs.

sections.title: main dispatcher
sections.explanation: `main` handles `--version` and help, then dispatches the first argument to the matching `cmd_*` function with a plain if-chain. Unknown commands return the framework's usage exit code, and `raise SystemExit(main())` makes the module runnable directly.

odrl_agent/app.py.overview: The FastAPI application factory for NL2ODRL Studio. `create_app` assembles the app with error handling, a request-observing middleware, cookie or Bearer authentication, and every `/api/*` route, delegating real work to `web.RunRegistry` and `publish`. It is the HTTP half of tour step 2.

sections.title: Module docs and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring is the API reference: sessions, convert, runs and SSE events, the draft review queue, policies, usage, settings, metrics and health. Imports pull in FastAPI, auth helpers and observability utilities, and `METRICS.describe` registers a counter for reviewer decisions.

sections.title: ApiError and app setup
sections.explanation: `ApiError` carries an HTTP status, a short code and a hint, so every error has one JSON shape. `create_app` takes the repo root and optional dependencies (UI dir, output dir, registry, sessions) for easy testing. The comment on sessions explains the `is not None` check: `SessionStore` defines `__len__`, so an empty store would be falsy.

sections.title: Error handler and middleware
sections.explanation: The exception handler turns `ApiError` into JSON with optional extra headers. The `_observe` middleware assigns or reuses an `X-Request-ID`, times the request, records Prometheus counters and histograms under the route template (not the raw URL, so labels stay low-cardinality), and emits one JSON log line with a truncated tenant fingerprint.

sections.title: Auth dependencies and helpers
sections.explanation: `principal` is a dependency that loads the key state from the database, authenticates via header or cookie, and enforces the CSRF header for cookie sessions. `json_body` caps bodies at 64 KiB and returns clean `E_CONFIG` errors. `own_snapshot` hides runs that belong to another tenant by answering 404.

sections.title: Health, session, settings routes
sections.explanation: `/api/healthz` reports queue counts without auth. Login validates the key, sets an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=strict` session cookie (with `secure` for HTTPS or an env flag), and returns a local session when no keys exist. Logout revokes the session; settings are read and written per tenant, with config errors mapped to 400.

sections.title: Convert and run routes
sections.explanation: `POST /api/convert` validates the body and starts a run in a thread pool, translating `BusyError` into `429` with `Retry-After`. `GET /api/runs` lists runs and `GET /api/runs/{run_key}` returns a snapshot, adding the draft and, once finished, the stored review decision.

sections.title: Server-Sent Events stream
sections.explanation: An async generator polls the registry every `SSE_POLL_SECONDS` and emits `status`, `trace` and finally `end` frames, sending only events not yet delivered. It stops on completion, on the hard time cap or when the client disconnects, and sends keep-alive comments so proxies do not close the stream.

sections.title: Review queue and publish
sections.explanation: `GET /api/drafts` lists drafts awaiting review, and `POST /api/runs/{run_key}/publish` hands the reviewer's decision, reason and optional edited IR to `publish_module.decide` in a thread. A run that is still converting gets 409, `PublishError` maps to its own status and code, and each decision increments a metric and writes a log line.

sections.title: Policies, usage, metrics, static UI
sections.explanation: Remaining routes list published pairs, per-key usage and Prometheus text. A catch-all `/api/{rest:path}` route returns a JSON 404 so unknown API paths never fall through to the static UI. When a built `ui/` directory exists it is mounted at `/`, and `_query` flattens query parameters into lists.

odrl_agent/web.py.overview: Service core behind the HTTP layer: constants and limits, API-key storage, request validation, building inline scenario runs, executing and recording conversions, tenant-scoped queries, the bounded `RunRegistry` worker queue, per-tenant model settings and the Uvicorn launcher. It supports the service half of tour step 2.

sections.title: Docs, imports, constants
sections.explanation: The docstring lists the module's duties. Constants fix the base scenario, input limit (4000 characters), queue defaults and SSE timing, and note that each is overridable by environment. The comment on `API_KEYS_ENV` explains the gate: it is off only while no keys exist anywhere, and it fails closed afterwards.

sections.title: Key state and request validation
sections.explanation: `_key_state` returns env keys, valid fingerprints and whether the gate is on; once a key has ever been issued, the gate stays on even if all are revoked. `validate_convert` strictly checks types and ranges for text, policy variant, seed and step count, rejecting booleans as ints. `build_inline_run` copies the base scenario, injects the pasted text as an untrusted doc and computes the run id and output paths.

sections.title: Trace reading and snapshots
sections.explanation: Helpers read trace events, sum token usage, summarize saves, extract the draft, and build and record snapshots into SQLite. The trace JSONL files stay the immutable artifact; the database holds the queryable summary.

sections.title: run_and_store
sections.explanation: Runs one conversion with either a live `LlmConfig` or a scripted transport, then runs the scenario invariants over the trace and state. A failed verdict gets a reference patch proposal, and the hash chain is verified. Model configuration and verifier errors become `error` snapshots with `E_MODEL_API` or `E_RUN` instead of exceptions, and the result is always persisted.

sections.title: Database, keys and queries
sections.explanation: Opens the database and creates sidecar tables for tenants and API keys, so upgrades of the framework never touch attribution. Keys are stored only as fingerprints. Run, pair and usage queries are scoped by key fingerprint, and `billing_lines` produces vendor-neutral line items.

sections.title: BusyError and RunRegistry
sections.explanation: `RunRegistry` is a bounded worker pool with a FIFO queue. When full it raises `BusyError` carrying a `Retry-After` estimated from an exponentially weighted mean run time. Finished runs are evicted by TTL and by count, after which snapshots come from the database, which keeps memory bounded. State is guarded by a lock.

sections.title: Query flags
sections.explanation: `_query_flags` turns URL query parameters into a flags dict used by the list endpoints.

sections.title: Per-tenant model settings
sections.explanation: `ServerSettings` keeps live-model overrides in memory per tenant, never in `os.environ`, so one tenant cannot change another tenant's endpoint or key. `apply_model_settings` validates each field, runs `validate_base_url` as an SSRF guard (see `netguard.py`), and `model_status` reports configuration without revealing the key.

sections.title: serve_ui launcher
sections.explanation: Opens the database once to create tables, configures logging, builds the app with `create_app`, and runs Uvicorn with access logging disabled in favour of the app's own JSON logs.

odrl_agent/ir.py.overview: Defines the typed policy intermediate representation (`PolicyIR`) as Pydantic models. It is the contract between the model, which supplies meaning, and the compiler, which supplies ODRL syntax, so malformed or out-of-vocabulary model output is rejected here instead of at SHACL time. It is the focus of tour step 3.

sections.title: Vocabulary tuples and Literals
sections.explanation: Lists the allowed actions, left operands, operators, policy types and value types, once as tuples (used to build prompts) and once as `Literal` types (used for validation and the JSON Schema). The two copies are kept in sync by a test against the bundled ontology, which is why the duplication is tolerated.

sections.title: Typing rules and patterns
sections.explanation: `OPERAND_VALUE_TYPES` records which value types each left operand may carry (for example `count` takes integers and `elapsedTime` takes durations). Ordering operators require ordered types. Regexes for ISO durations, integers, decimals and IRIs, and a maximum constraint depth of 3, back the checks.

sections.title: Base model, SpanRef, check_value
sections.explanation: `_Model` forbids extra fields so the model cannot smuggle in unknown keys. `SpanRef` holds a verbatim quote, and the ground stage later fills its offsets. `check_value` validates a literal string against its declared type and returns a readable message, which later feeds repair prompts.

sections.title: Constraints and nesting depth
sections.explanation: `ConstraintIR` is one atomic `left operator right` triple whose `model_validator` cross-checks the literal, the operand's allowed types and the operator. `LogicalConstraintIR` combines two or more constraints, and a discriminated union on `kind` lets Pydantic pick the right class. `model_rebuild` resolves the forward reference, and `constraint_depth` with `_check_depth` limits recursion.

sections.title: Duties and rules
sections.explanation: `DutyIR` describes an obligation attached to a permission. `RuleIR` covers permission, prohibition and obligation, and its validator enforces that only permissions carry duties, obligations need an assignee, and party names are not blank.

sections.title: Ambiguity and assumption records
sections.explanation: `AmbiguityFlag` and `AssumptionRecord` let the extractor flag what the text leaves open or what it filled in, instead of inventing facts. The publish gate later routes any draft with such entries to human review.

sections.title: PolicyIR root model
sections.explanation: The root model holds an `analysis` field written before the structured fields, the policy type, parties, rules, ambiguities and assumptions. Its validator requires an assigner for Offer and Agreement, an assignee for Agreement, and valid `rule_index` references. `is_compilable` is true when there is at least one rule, and `ir_json_schema` exposes the schema that a snapshot test pins.

sections.title: Wire schema unrolling
sections.explanation: Some OpenAI-compatible providers reject recursive or deeply nested JSON Schemas. `_unroll` inlines every `$ref` and cuts recursion at a limit, dropping branches that would exceed it, and `schema_depth` measures nesting. `wire_schema` returns the flattened schema sent to the model, while replies are still validated against the full `PolicyIR`.

odrl_agent/extractor.py.overview: Turns natural-language policy text into a validated `PolicyIR` using one structured model call, plus a decompose call for complex inputs and a repair call that receives validation violations. The model never sees tools, Turtle or JSON-LD. This is the main logic of tour step 4.

sections.title: Docs, imports and heuristics
sections.explanation: The docstring explains that source text reaches the model as quoted, untrusted data, and that a fast and a strong model are routed by complexity (both default to the same id). Two regexes detect complexity markers such as `unless` and `must not`, and split sentences deterministically.

sections.title: System and decompose prompts
sections.explanation: The system prompt tells the model that source text is data, requires verbatim quotes for each rule, forbids inventing parties or numbers, and requires ambiguities and assumptions to be recorded. It also specifies typed values and when to use permission, prohibition or obligation. A separate prompt asks only for a clause split.

sections.title: Result types and classify
sections.explanation: `ClauseSplit`, `ModelRoute` and `ExtractResult` are small containers. `classify` is a deterministic, model-free heuristic returning COMPLEX when there are many sentences, several markers or long text, so routing costs no extra call.

sections.title: Prompt and error helpers
sections.explanation: `_system_prompt` injects the vocabulary lists from `ir.py`. `_source_block` wraps the text in `<untrusted_source>` tags, and `format_validation_errors` flattens Pydantic errors into stable `path: message` strings that the repair prompt can quote. `parse_ir` validates a raw reply into either a `PolicyIR` or those errors.

sections.title: Extractor class
sections.explanation: `decompose` falls back to the sentence split if the reply is invalid and drops clauses that are not verbatim substrings of the text. `extract` picks the model route and validates the reply. `repair` sends the previous IR and violations to the strong model with instructions that allow removing or narrowing rules but forbid adding permissions or removing prohibitions, duties or constraints. The class never compiles or publishes.

odrl_agent/llm.py.overview: A small httpx client for OpenAI-compatible chat endpoints that returns one JSON object matching a JSON Schema. It adds retry with exponential backoff, usage accounting and strict response checks, and is built per run from an immutable config. It is part of tour step 4.

sections.title: Docs and constants
sections.explanation: The docstring lists the retry policy: transient statuses (429, 500, 502, 503, 504) and transport errors back off exponentially and honor `Retry-After`, while other HTTP errors fail fast. Constants set 4 attempts, 0.5 s base backoff capped at 8 s, a 60 s timeout and an 8000-token default.

sections.title: Errors and usage accounting
sections.explanation: `LlmError` carries the code `E_MODEL_API` and `LlmNotConfiguredError` marks a missing endpoint or key. `LlmUsage` accumulates calls, attempts and token counts, ignoring values that are not integers.

sections.title: StructuredLlm configuration
sections.explanation: A dataclass holds endpoint, key, timeouts, retry settings, an injectable httpx `transport` for tests, and an injectable `sleep`. `from_config` duck-types a config object so the client has no dependency on the adapter module, and no process-global environment is read here.

sections.title: Retry delay
sections.explanation: `_retry_delay` uses the `Retry-After` header when it parses, clamped to the 8 s cap, and otherwise doubles the base backoff for each attempt.

sections.title: complete_json request loop
sections.explanation: Builds a `json_schema` response-format request at temperature 0 and posts it in a bounded retry loop. A non-transient HTTP error raises at once, and the final attempt does not sleep. Afterwards it checks that the response has `choices[0].message`, rejects `finish_reason == length` as truncated, and requires a bare JSON object; there is deliberately no brace-scraping fallback.

odrl_agent/netguard.py.overview: An SSRF guard for user-supplied model endpoints. It rejects unsafe base URLs before the server will ever send a request to them, which matters because tenants can set their own endpoint through the settings API. It belongs to tour step 4.

sections.title: Constants and error type
sections.explanation: Defines the optional allowlist environment variable `NL2ODRL_ALLOWED_LLM_HOSTS`, a few blocked cloud metadata names and `UnsafeBaseUrlError`.

sections.title: Blocked address test
sections.explanation: `_blocked` treats link-local (which includes the 169.254.x.x metadata range), unspecified, multicast and reserved addresses as unsafe. Loopback is intentionally allowed for local model servers.

sections.title: validate_base_url
sections.explanation: Checks the scheme, requires a host, rejects embedded credentials and metadata names, and applies the allowlist when set. It then resolves the hostname and rejects any address that falls in a blocked range, unwrapping IPv4-mapped IPv6 first. Names that do not resolve are not rejected here, and the function returns the URL without its trailing slash.

odrl_agent/compiler.py.overview: Deterministic compiler from `PolicyIR` to ODRL 2.2 JSON-LD plus an RDF graph. It involves no model, network or clock, so the same IR always produces identical output. Code, not the model, owns IRIs and literal types. This is the heart of tour step 5.

sections.title: Docs, imports, constants
sections.explanation: The docstring states the guarantees: byte-identical canonical JSON-LD and an isomorphic graph for the same IR, validated offline using the bundled context. Constants define the `urn:nl2odrl:` prefixes for parties, assets and policies and the ODRL namespace.

sections.title: IRI minting and canonical JSON
sections.explanation: `mint_iri` keeps names that are already absolute IRIs and otherwise builds a URN from a case-folded, hyphenated slug. Non-ASCII characters are percent-encoded rather than folded, so look-alike names stay distinct IRIs. `canonical_json` sorts keys with compact separators for hashing and comparison.

sections.title: Literals and constraints
sections.explanation: `_literal` emits plain strings, `{"@id"}` for IRIs and typed `@value` objects for the rest. `_constraint` builds atomic or logical constraints, using an `@list` for `andSequence` so order is preserved.

sections.title: Actions, duties and rules
sections.explanation: `_action` returns a plain action or a refined action with `rdf:value` and `refinement`. `_duty` and `_rule` build the Permission, Prohibition or Duty nodes, mint party and asset IRIs, and omit assignee or assigner when they repeat the policy-level value. A permission or prohibition with no target raises `CompileError`.

sections.title: Policy uid and compile_doc
sections.explanation: When no uid is given, `_policy_uid` hashes the canonical IR (excluding `analysis` and `ambiguities`) with SHA-256, so identical policies get identical ids. `compile_doc` assembles the document with the ODRL context, type, uid, conflict strategy, parties and one array per modality.

sections.title: Graph verification and compile_ir
sections.explanation: `_verify_graph` counts permission, prohibition and obligation triples in the parsed graph and fails loudly if JSON-LD processing dropped anything. `compile_ir` is the public entry returning both the document and graph.

odrl_agent/odrl.py.overview: Offline ODRL 2.2 validation. It loads the bundled ontology, JSON-LD context and SHACL shapes from `schemas/`, converts JSON-LD to an RDF graph without fetching anything, and validates it with pySHACL. It supplies the ontology, context and RDF conversion for tour step 5.

sections.title: Docs and constants
sections.explanation: The docstring promises no wall-clock, network or model use and notes that the older subset validator was retired. Constants set the canonical context URL, the allowed policy types and the synthetic attacker principal used by the poisoned fixture, with a note that it is not an email address so redaction keeps it as evidence.

sections.title: Loading the ontology
sections.explanation: `_repo_file` searches upward for a `schemas/` file. The ontology is parsed once at import, and the module raises `ImportError` if Set, Offer or Agreement are not Policy subclasses, so vocabulary drift fails early. `ontology_terms` lists individuals of a given class.

sections.title: Attacker-grant scan
sections.explanation: `contains_attacker_grant` recursively scans every string in a document so a smuggled grant cannot hide in a nested constraint or duty.

sections.title: Local context and shapes
sections.explanation: Loads the bundled `odrl-2.2.jsonld` as `LOCAL_CONTEXT` and parses the SHACL shapes once. A fixed relative base IRI makes bare names resolve identically on every machine.

sections.title: Offline JSON-LD parsing
sections.explanation: `_localize_context` swaps the canonical context URL for the bundled copy and refuses any other remote context. `jsonld_to_graph` then parses the document with rdflib, so validation never fetches anything.

sections.title: validate_odrl
sections.explanation: Never raises: it returns `(valid, errors)`. It checks the context and policy type, parses the graph, runs pySHACL without inference against the full shapes, and builds sorted, deduplicated messages that include the failing property name.

schemas/odrl-2.2.ttl.overview: The bundled W3C ODRL 2.2 ontology in Turtle (2274 lines). `odrl.py` parses it at import time to confirm policy types and expose vocabulary terms, and the SHACL shapes check output against its terms. It is the standard reference in tour step 6.

sections.title: Prefixes and ontology header
sections.explanation: Declares namespace prefixes (`odrl`, `rdf`, `rdfs`, `skos`, `owl`, `xsd`, `dct`, `schema`, `foaf`, `vcard`, `cc`) and the `owl:Ontology` resource for ODRL Version 2.2 with its creators, description and license.

sections.title: SKOS collections
sections.explanation: Groups terms into `skos:Collection` resources (policy, rule, conflict, asset, party, action, constraint, operand and operator groups, and deprecated terms). They exist mainly to organize the vocabulary document and are not used for validation.

sections.title: Core classes and properties
sections.explanation: The core profile: assets, parties, the `:Policy` class and its subclasses, Permission, Prohibition, Duty, Action and Constraint classes, and properties such as `:action`, `:constraint`, `:duty` and `:operator`. About 45 `owl:Class` and 46 object-property declarations appear in the file as a whole, and this region holds the main ones.

sections.title: Operators and left operands
sections.explanation: Defines the `:Operator` class and individuals such as `eq`, `gt` and `isAnyOf`, then the `:LeftOperand` class and its individuals (for example `:dateTime`, `:count`, `:purpose`). Their local names are the same lists mirrored in `ir.py`.

sections.title: Actions
sections.explanation: Declares the standard action individuals, from `use` and `display` to `synchronize`, with `includedIn` hierarchy links that the Z3 reasoner uses for action-overlap checks.

sections.title: Functions, policies, scopes
sections.explanation: Defines party functions (assigner, assignee and the like), policy-type individuals (Set, Offer, Agreement and others) and party or asset scopes.

sections.title: Deprecated and collective terms
sections.explanation: Keeps deprecated terms for backward compatibility, the collective vocabulary, and annotation-property declarations that keep the ontology within OWL DL.

schemas/odrl-2.2.jsonld.overview: The bundled W3C ODRL 2.2 JSON-LD context (200 lines). It maps short JSON keys such as `permission`, `target` and `leftOperand` to full ODRL IRIs and declares how values are typed. `odrl.py` substitutes it for the remote context URL so validation never needs a network. It is part of tour step 6.

sections.title: Namespace prefixes
sections.explanation: Opens the `@context` object and declares prefixes for `odrl`, `rdf`, `rdfs`, `owl`, `skos`, `dct`, `xsd`, `vcard`, `foaf`, `schema` and `cc`.

sections.title: Keywords, policy types, assets, parties
sections.explanation: Aliases `uid` to `@id` and `type` to `@type`, then maps policy classes (Policy, Set, Offer, Agreement and others), conflict terms, asset terms such as `target`, and party properties such as `assignee`, `assigner` and the role pairs. Properties holding references are typed `@type: @id`.

sections.title: Actions and rules
sections.explanation: Maps `action` (vocabulary-typed), Permission and Prohibition classes and their properties, `obligation`, and the individual action terms starting with `use`.

sections.title: Duties and constraints
sections.explanation: Defines `Duty` and `duty`, then `Constraint`, `LogicalConstraint`, `constraint`, `refinement`, and the `operator` and `leftOperand` properties, which are typed `@vocab` so a bare string like `eq` expands to an ODRL IRI.

sections.title: Operands, operators, closing
sections.explanation: Lists left-operand terms such as `count` and `dateTime`, relational operators such as `eq`, and logical operators such as `and`, then closes the context. The compiler output only works offline because these mappings are available locally.

schemas/odrl-2.2-shapes.ttl.overview: SHACL shapes for the ODRL 2.2 core profile, written in Turtle. They validate the RDF graph obtained by parsing the compiler's JSON-LD output, so a compiled policy can be checked locally with no network access. This is the standard that the tour step on ODRL vocabulary and SHACL refers to.

sections.title: Prefixes and design notes
sections.explanation: Declares the `sh`, `odrl`, `rdf`, `xsd` and `ex` prefixes. The comment explains that every node in the validated graph is explicitly typed, so shapes can target classes without RDFS inference. Extra properties are allowed (no `sh:closed`), and vocabulary lists are pinned to the bundled ontology by a test.

sections.title: Action vocabulary list
sections.explanation: `ex:ActionTerms` lists every ODRL 2.2 action IRI as an RDF list. It acts as a single reference copy of the vocabulary that tests can compare with `schemas/odrl-2.2.ttl`. The same list is repeated inline in `ex:ActionValueShape`, because SHACL `sh:in` needs a literal list.

sections.title: Policy, Offer and Agreement shapes
sections.explanation: `ex:PolicyShape` requires an IRI-identified Set, Offer or Agreement with at least one permission, prohibition or obligation. It also limits `odrl:conflict` to perm, prohibit or invalid and requires single-IRI assigner and assignee. `OfferShape` and `AgreementShape` add the rule that an assigner (and for Agreements an assignee) must exist at policy level or on every rule, using the `HasAssigner` and `HasAssignee` helper shapes.

sections.title: Rule and prohibition shapes
sections.explanation: Rules are found with `sh:targetObjectsOf`, following the properties that point at them, because ODRL 2.2 does not require an explicit `rdf:type` on a rule. A rule needs exactly one action and an IRI target. `ProhibitionShape` forbids any duty on a prohibition.

sections.title: Action value shape
sections.explanation: An action is valid if it is a vocabulary IRI, or a blank node holding an `rdf:value` from the vocabulary plus at least one `odrl:refinement`. The second branch supports refined actions such as `use` limited by a constraint. The long IRI list is duplicated in both branches, which is verbose but required by SHACL.

sections.title: Duty and obligation shapes
sections.explanation: `DutyShape` applies to objects of `odrl:duty` and `odrl:obligation` and requires exactly one vocabulary action. `ObligationShape` adds that a policy-level obligation must name an assignee, since otherwise nobody is bound to act.

sections.title: Constraint shapes
sections.explanation: A constraint is identified by the property pointing at it (constraint, refinement, and/or/xone), so third-party documents without an explicit Constraint type still validate. `ConstraintValueShape` uses `sh:xone` to demand either an atomic or a logical form. `AtomicConstraintShape` restricts the left operand and operator to the ODRL 2.2 vocabularies and requires a right operand. Literal datatypes are checked in the IR layer instead.

sections.title: Logical and typed constraints
sections.explanation: `LogicalConstraintShape` needs exactly one of and/or/xone with at least two members, or an `andSequence` list walked with a property path over `rdf:rest` and `rdf:first`. `AtomicOrLogicalShape` accepts members of such lists. `TypedConstraintShape` gives precise error messages for nodes explicitly typed as `odrl:Constraint`.

odrl_agent/grounder.py.overview: Implements the entity grounding and least-privilege gate. It checks that parties and assets in a PolicyIR exist in an entity catalog or in the source text, rejects wildcard or external grants, and detects permissions supported only by prompt-injected text. It never calls a model and never widens a policy. It corresponds to the grounding half of the Grounding and Z3 Reasoning tour step.

sections.title: Module purpose and issue codes
sections.explanation: The docstring defines three checks: grounded names, least privilege, and authorship of grants. Stable string codes such as `BROAD_GRANT`, `INJECTED_GRANT` and `SUSPICIOUS_NAME` are defined here and collected in `ISSUE_CODES`. `WILDCARD_NAMES` and the compiled `_INJECTION_PATTERNS` drive detection of public principals and instruction-like text.

sections.title: Name normalization and catalog
sections.explanation: `normalize_name` canonicalizes text with Unicode normalization before comparison, and `_suspicious` flags names that look deceptive. `CatalogEntry` is a frozen record and `EntityCatalog` maps names and aliases to IRIs, loadable from a dict or file. Normalizing first is what lets homoglyph names be caught.

sections.title: Issue and report types
sections.explanation: `GroundingIssue` carries a code, detail, rule index and field. `GroundingReport` collects issues and resolved names and exposes `grounded`, `codes`, `as_dict` and `messages`. Any issue blocks auto-publication, so there is no warning level.

sections.title: Source-text helpers
sections.explanation: Reads trusted party names from the `NL2ODRL_TRUSTED_PARTIES` environment variable. `injected_ranges` finds character spans that match injection patterns, and `_mentions`, `_aliases` and `_overlaps` locate a name in the source and test whether it falls inside an injected span. `_constraint_values` flattens nested logical constraints to atomic ones.

sections.title: Grounder setup and name resolution
sections.explanation: `Grounder.__init__` takes an optional catalog, an `allow_external` flag and trusted parties. `_resolve` applies the checks in order: wildcard grant, suspicious name, catalog lookup (substituting the IRI), trusted party, then a mention search in the source. A name that appears only inside injected text yields `INJECTED_GRANT`.

sections.title: Grounding a whole policy
sections.explanation: `ground` deep-copies the IR so the input is never mutated, merges detected injected ranges with caller-supplied untrusted ranges, then resolves the policy-level assigner and assignee. It treats the assignee as a grant if any rule is a permission. It returns the new IR together with the report.

sections.title: Per-rule checks
sections.explanation: `_ground_rule` flags rules with no source span and permissions whose spans all lie in injected text. It resolves assignee, assigner, target and duty assignees, and reports a permission with no target as a broad grant. It also reports a `recipient` constraint whose value is a wildcard.

sections.title: Convenience wrapper
sections.explanation: `ground_entities` builds a `Grounder` and calls `ground` in one step, forwarding the optional `allow_external` flag.

odrl_agent/reasoning.py.overview: Uses Z3 to find logical problems in a PolicyIR: constraints that can never hold, permissions that overlap prohibitions, and obligations that are prohibited. It encodes constraint trees and uses the ODRL action hierarchy from the bundled ontology. This is the formal reasoning half of the Grounding and Z3 Reasoning tour step.

sections.title: Analyses and constants
sections.explanation: The docstring lists the three analyses and states a safety goal: operators Z3 cannot model are left unconstrained, so the engine may miss a conflict but never invents one. The constants include the ontology path, a duration regex, operands that must be non-negative and the finding codes.

sections.title: Action hierarchy and value parsing
sections.explanation: `action_parents` reads `odrl:includedIn` relations from the ontology once (cached with `lru_cache`). `ancestors` and `includes` answer whether a broader action covers a narrower one. The `_duration_seconds`, `_epoch` and `_numeric` helpers turn dates, datetimes and ISO durations into floats so Z3 can compare them.

sections.title: Z3 constraint encoder
sections.explanation: `_Encoder` keeps one Z3 variable per left operand, adds axioms such as `count >= 0` and `percentage <= 100`, and turns atomic constraints into comparisons. Constraints it cannot model become a fresh free boolean, which keeps the result sound. Logical nodes map to And, Or and a pseudo-boolean equality for `xone`.

sections.title: Thread-safe solving
sections.explanation: Z3's default context is global and not thread-safe, so every Z3 object is created and freed under `_Z3_LOCK`. `_solve` sets a two-second timeout and treats `unknown` as satisfiable, again to avoid inventing conflicts. `satisfiable` is the public entry point.

sections.title: Finding and report types
sections.explanation: `Finding` records a code, detail, involved rule indexes and a path. `ReasoningReport` separates unsatisfiable-constraint findings from conflicts and provides `ok`, `as_dict` and `messages` for the pipeline and review gate.

sections.title: Policy analysis
sections.explanation: `analyze` first reports rules and duties whose constraints are unsatisfiable. It then pairs each permission with each prohibition that includes its action. When rules can overlap and no `conflict` strategy is set it raises a deontic conflict, or a hierarchy conflict for different actions. Finally it flags obligations and duties that a prohibition forbids, regardless of strategy.

odrl_agent/pipeline.py.overview: The fixed-stage conversion pipeline that replaced the earlier ReAct loop. The model is called only to extract, decompose and repair; grounding, compilation, SHACL and Z3 checks, persistence and the publish decision are plain code. It also records trace events and SDK events and enforces a shrink-only repair rule. It is the orchestrator described in the Pipeline and Publish Gate tour step.

sections.title: Pipeline design notes
sections.explanation: The docstring lists the stages (ingest, optional decompose, extract, ground, compile, verify, up to two repairs, draft). It states that repair is shrink-only: a repaired IR may drop or narrow permissions but may not add one or remove a restriction.

sections.title: Constants and PolicyDraft
sections.explanation: Defines the pipeline id, `MAX_REPAIRS = 2`, the stage names and `PipelineError`. `PolicyDraft` is the result object handed to reviewers: status (ready, needs_review, no_rules, failed), the ODRL document and IR, errors, ambiguities, grounding and reasoning reports, and an `auto_publish` flag that is true only for a fully clean draft.

sections.title: Span grounding and widening check
sections.explanation: `locate` finds a quoted span in the source, exactly and then ignoring case and whitespace. `ground` fills span offsets and reports rules whose quotes are not found. `widening` compares an old and a new IR and returns reasons the new one grants more, such as a new permission, removed prohibition or duty, or a relaxed conflict strategy. The review gate reuses it for reviewer edits.

sections.title: Per-run trace plumbing
sections.explanation: `_Run` writes the legacy hash-chained trace events that the verifiers judge, and mirrors each stage, model call and tool call into the AgentCrash SDK run when one is attached. Its `fault` method asks the SDK whether a chaos fault fires at a boundary. Keeping this here lets `convert` stay focused on the logic.

sections.title: Model calls and holding drafts
sections.explanation: `_usage_delta` computes token usage per call. `_call` wraps a model call at the LLM boundary and simulates a `timeout_after_commit` fault by billing a call, discarding its result and retrying once. `_hold` withdraws auto-publication and moves a ready draft to needs_review.

sections.title: Safe single publish
sections.explanation: `_publish` validates the document, reads the record version, re-reads it just before writing, and holds the draft if another writer changed the version (check-then-act). It writes with `expected_version`. If a write acknowledgement is lost, it reads the record back instead of writing again, which keeps saves exactly-once.

sections.title: convert: routing and extraction
sections.explanation: `convert` runs the semantic stages without persistence, so it can be unit-tested. It strips the input, classifies it as simple or complex, decomposes complex text into clauses with the fast model, and extracts with the strong model for complex input.

sections.title: convert: ground, verify, repair loop
sections.explanation: Each pass rejects a widening repair and falls back to the last good IR, grounds spans, compiles, runs SHACL validation and Z3 analysis, and collects violations. If violations remain and fewer than `MAX_REPAIRS` attempts were used, the strong model is asked to repair the previous IR.

sections.title: convert: shrink-only fallback and draft
sections.explanation: After the loop, permissions that are ungrounded, target-less, assigned to nobody or backed only by injected text are dropped, while prohibitions and obligations are always kept. A `missing_assignee` ambiguity is added when a grant had no party. The final IR is compiled and validated, and the draft is marked ready only when nothing needs a human.

sections.title: run_conversion entry point
sections.explanation: Builds the extractor, ledger, tool registry, trace writer and SDK run, then writes run_start and run_end events around `convert`. A poisoned-source fault can replace the input text. Only an auto-publish draft is saved, through `_publish`. The trace is checked with `strict_validate` before the run summary is returned.

odrl_agent/publish.py.overview: The human-in-the-loop publish gate. Drafts that the pipeline did not auto-publish wait here, and a reviewer can approve, edit or reject them with a reason. Every verdict is recomputed at decision time and each run can be decided only once. It completes the Pipeline and Publish Gate tour step.

sections.title: Gate rules and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring defines the three decisions. Approve is blocked by SHACL failures or remaining conflicts, edit re-grounds and recompiles a reviewer IR, and reject closes the draft. It states that nothing is trusted from the stored draft and that a draft is published at most once.

sections.title: Table SQL and constants
sections.explanation: `PUBLICATIONS_SQL` defines the `nl2odrl_publications` table with `run_key` as primary key, which is what enforces one decision per run. It also stores the reviewer fingerprint, widening notes, alerts and the published document and IR. `MAX_REASON` caps reason length.

sections.title: PublishError
sections.explanation: A `ValueError` subclass that carries a machine code, a hint and an HTTP status so the web layer can turn a refusal into a reply.

sections.title: Event and decision helpers
sections.explanation: `ensure_tables` creates the publications table on demand. `run_end_detail`, `draft_of` and `source_of` pull the stored draft and source text from the run's trace events. `decision_for` reads a prior decision for a run.

sections.title: Review result
sections.explanation: `Review` holds freshly computed verdicts for a candidate document. `blocking` lists reasons that stop publication: no document, SHACL errors or logical conflicts. Alerts, such as ambiguities, do not block, because a human may vouch for them.

sections.title: Recomputing the review
sections.explanation: `review_draft` validates the stored or edited IR against the PolicyIR schema (a bad edit raises `E_SCHEMA`), resolves spans, grounds entities, compiles, validates with SHACL and runs Z3 analysis. For an edit it also computes which grants were widened, which is recorded but allowed.

sections.title: Recording a decision
sections.explanation: `decide` validates the inputs, refuses auto-published, missing or already-decided drafts, and blocks approvals and edits that fail the review with `E_BLOCKED`. It inserts the publication row and, for approve and edit, an `odrl_docs` row in one transaction. A unique-key violation from a racing second decision becomes `E_DECIDED`.

sections.title: Listing held drafts
sections.explanation: `list_drafts` joins runs, their `run_end` event, decisions and tenant fingerprints to return the review queue, newest first. It clamps the limit to 1..500, filters by tenant scope and skips auto-published drafts. All values are passed as query parameters.

odrl_agent/db.py.overview: The SQLite query layer for runs, trace events, verdicts, patches and ODRL documents, using only the standard library. The JSONL traces remain the immutable record, and this module is what the API and UI read. It is part of the Pipeline and Publish Gate step because the publish gate stores decisions and documents in the same database.

sections.title: Module notes and schema
sections.explanation: The schema creates `runs`, `events`, `verdicts`, `patches` and `odrl_docs` with foreign keys back to `runs.run_key`, plus indexes on creation time and on run and sequence. All statements use `IF NOT EXISTS`, so the script can run repeatedly.

sections.title: Connection and migration
sections.explanation: `connect` opens SQLite with `Row` access and foreign keys enabled. `migrate` runs the schema script and stores `SCHEMA_VERSION` the first time, returning the stored version afterward.

sections.title: Insert a finished run
sections.explanation: `insert_run` replaces a run row and writes its events, verdicts, patch and ODRL documents from one record. Values are bound as parameters and complex fields are stored as sorted JSON.

sections.title: Run listing
sections.explanation: `_RUN_COLUMNS` and `_run_row` shape a stored row, decoding fault JSON and the chain flag. `list_runs` builds a filtered, newest-first summary query with optional scenario, verdict and status filters. Filters are added as bound parameters rather than string-formatted values.

sections.title: Full run snapshot
sections.explanation: `get_run` rebuilds a response shaped like the live API: events with decoded injector and policy decisions, verdict rows, the patch, saved documents, token totals and any error. The UI can therefore show a stored run the same way as one still running.

sections.title: ODRL document pairs
sections.explanation: `list_odrl_docs` returns NL-to-ODRL pairs for the Policies view, with optional scenario, validity and attacker filters and a limit.

ui-react/src/main.tsx.overview: The React entry point. It mounts the `App` component into the `#root` element inside `StrictMode`. It is the start of the React Studio UI tour step.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Imports `StrictMode`, the React 18 `createRoot` API, the `App` component and the global stylesheet.

sections.title: Mount the app
sections.explanation: Creates the root on the `#root` element, using a non-null assertion, and renders `App` inside `StrictMode`. StrictMode adds development-time checks, such as double-invoked effects, that help find side-effect bugs.

ui-react/src/App.tsx.overview: The studio's main component file. It defines four views (Convert, Review, Policies, Runs), a model setup dialog and helpers for showing JSON and run outcomes. All server access goes through the typed client in `api.ts`. It is the core of the React Studio UI tour step.

sections.title: Imports and constants
sections.explanation: Imports React hooks and the typed API client with its interfaces. Declares the `Tab` union, the `ATTACKER` marker string used to highlight a poisoned client name, and an example sentence for the Convert view.

sections.title: Rendering helpers
sections.explanation: `highlightJson` HTML-escapes a pretty-printed value before wrapping keys and strings in spans, so the markup is safe to inject. `markAttacker` highlights lines naming the attacker. `outcomeOf` turns a run snapshot into a one-line message covering queued, running, error, held-for-review, pass and the specific failed invariants.

sections.title: Policies view
sections.explanation: Lists NL and ODRL pairs with scenario, validity and attacker filters. A memoized `useCallback` loader calls `api.pairs`, updates the scenario options and shows errors in a status note.

sections.title: Model setup dialog
sections.explanation: A dialog for saving the model base URL and API key through `api.saveSettings`, so the live model can be configured from the UI.

sections.title: Convert view
sections.explanation: Takes natural-language text, starts a conversion with `api.convert` and follows progress with `followRun`. It opens the setup dialog when no model is configured and links to the finished run.

sections.title: Run view
sections.explanation: Shows a run's trace events, verdict rows, saved documents and draft details. It can focus on a run chosen from another tab and clears that request through `onConsumed`.

sections.title: Source highlighting
sections.explanation: The `Highlighted` component marks the source-text spans that rules cite, so a reviewer can see which sentence produced which rule.

sections.title: Review view
sections.explanation: Loads held drafts and lets a reviewer approve, edit or reject each with a reason through `api.publish`. Server errors surface as `ApiError` with a code and detail, such as the blocking reasons the publish gate returns.

sections.title: App shell
sections.explanation: `App` holds the active tab, the run to focus and the model settings. It loads settings on mount and opens the setup dialog if the model is not configured. The sidebar, top bar and tabs share one `titles` map, and each view is mounted only while its tab is active.

ui-react/src/api.ts.overview: The typed client for the FastAPI backend. It declares TypeScript interfaces for the API payloads, an `ApiError` class, a shared `fetch` wrapper and an `api` object with one method per endpoint. It also provides `followRun`, which streams a run's progress. It keeps the UI and backend shapes aligned, as described in the React Studio UI tour step.

sections.title: Payload interfaces
sections.explanation: Interfaces for run specs, source spans, rules, the PolicyIR, drafts, review decisions, run snapshots, trace events, verdict rows, saved documents, model settings and the session. They mirror the backend JSON, so a field change on the server shows up as a compile error here.

sections.title: ApiError
sections.explanation: An `Error` subclass carrying the HTTP status, the server's error code and optional structured detail, so callers can show the server's hint and inspect details.

sections.title: JSON fetch wrapper
sections.explanation: `json<T>` sends `credentials: 'same-origin'` and an `X-Requested-With` header that the server requires as CSRF protection on cookie-authenticated writes. The comment says the key becomes an HttpOnly session cookie and is never put in localStorage. A non-OK response becomes an `ApiError`. `post` builds JSON POST options.

sections.title: Endpoint methods
sections.explanation: The `api` object has methods for login, logout, whoami, convert, run lookups, pairs, drafts, publish and settings. Each returns a typed promise and URL-encodes any run key placed in a path.

sections.title: Following a run
sections.explanation: `followRun` opens a Server-Sent Events stream and counts trace events until an `end` event arrives. If `EventSource` is missing, the stream errors or it times out, it falls back to polling once per second for up to 600 tries. A `settled` flag stops the stream from resolving twice.

sections.title: Number formatting
sections.explanation: `fmt` formats a number with US thousands separators and shows a dash when the value is missing.

ui-react/vite.config.ts.overview: The Vite build and dev-server configuration for the studio. It builds into the `ui` folder that the Python backend serves, and proxies API calls in development. It covers the build part of the React Studio UI tour step.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Imports the React plugin and `defineConfig`, which gives type checking for the config object.

sections.title: Build and dev server
sections.explanation: `base: './'` makes asset URLs relative, so the bundle works when served from the backend. The build writes to `../ui` and empties it first. The dev server runs on port 5173 and proxies `/api` to `localhost:8901`, avoiding CORS issues during development.

odrl_agent/bench/generate.py.overview: A deterministic generator for the 240-case Benchmark v1. Each case pairs a natural-language text with its gold PolicyIR, so the text and labels cannot drift apart. Cases are spread over five difficulty tiers and a manifest records a hash of the cases. It supports the Benchmark and Quality Gates tour step.

sections.title: Purpose and settings
sections.explanation: The docstring says vocabulary is kept disjoint from training data and fixtures, and that all cases in a group land in a single split to avoid near-duplicates across dev and test. `TIER_SHARES` fixes 240 cases across five tiers.

sections.title: Vocabulary pools
sections.explanation: Lists of invented parties, assets, action phrasings, regions, purposes and dates. The injection principals and Cyrillic homoglyph names serve the adversarial tier.

sections.title: Case-building helpers
sections.explanation: Small builders create spans, rules, atomic constraints and a gold IR, and `_case` assembles an id, tier, group, text, gold IR and expected flags. `_name` picks pool entries with a stride so cases vary deterministically without randomness.

sections.title: Tier 1 simple grants
sections.explanation: Generates plain single permissions in three phrasings across the core actions. The quote in the gold rule is the exact phrase from the text, which lets span grounding be tested.

sections.title: Tiers 2 and 3
sections.explanation: Tier 2 covers single constraints, prohibitions and duties (until, region, purpose, count, prohibit, duty, elapsed). Tier 3 covers compound cases such as split rules, two parties, alternatives, windows, conflicts and unsatisfiable constraints, with an assertion that family counts equal the tier share.

sections.title: Tiers 4 and 5
sections.explanation: Tier 4 holds ambiguous inputs, such as a missing assignee or target and vague terms like soon. Tier 5 holds adversarial inputs: ignore-previous, instruction tags, role overrides, JSON breakout, homoglyphs and wildcard notes.

sections.title: Assembling cases and splits
sections.explanation: `build_cases` concatenates the tiers, numbers the ids and assigns a split. `split_of` hashes the group name with SHA-256 to give roughly 30 percent dev and 70 percent test. `canonical` produces stable JSON for hashing.

sections.title: Manifest and writing
sections.explanation: `cases_sha` and `build_manifest` record the version, total, tier shares, split rule and per-group counts. `write` saves `cases.json` and `manifest.json` under `benchmarks/v1`. The runner later refuses cases that do not match the manifest hash.

odrl_agent/bench/runner.py.overview: Runs the real conversion pipeline over every benchmark case and builds the report. The report combines metrics, gate results, a baseline comparison and an identity block (version, hash, commit and pins) so a run can be reproduced. It connects generation to the metrics and gates in the Benchmark and Quality Gates tour step.

sections.title: Imports and factory type
sections.explanation: Imports the sibling `gates`, `generate`, `metrics` and `pins` modules and the pipeline's `convert`. `LlmFactory` is a callable that returns a fresh client for each case.

sections.title: Load verified cases
sections.explanation: `load_cases` reads `cases.json` and raises an error if its hash differs from the manifest. This prevents running against a hand-edited or stale benchmark.

sections.title: Run one case
sections.explanation: Builds a fresh LLM client, calls `convert` with a `Grounder` that has no trusted parties, so a party is grounded only if the text names it. An `LlmError` becomes a failed draft instead of aborting the run. It records the draft, calls, tokens, wall time and error.

sections.title: Run all cases
sections.explanation: Runs cases in order or on a thread pool when `workers` is above one. Each case gets its own client, which keeps threads from sharing state.

sections.title: Git commit lookup
sections.explanation: Reads `HEAD` with a 10-second timeout and returns `unknown` if git is missing or fails, so a report never fails over provenance.

sections.title: Build the report
sections.explanation: `report` computes overall and per-tier metrics, evaluates gates and adds regression rows against a baseline. With `enforce='regression'` only the baseline comparison can fail the run, though absolute gates are still listed as not enforced. It also lists failing cases with their false permissions.

odrl_agent/bench/metrics.py.overview: Pure functions that turn benchmark case results into the Phase 4.2 metrics (checkpoint F1, false-permission rate, ambiguity recall, latency percentiles and more). It reads predictions from each draft's final IR, the same IR the compiler consumed. The gates module compares these numbers to thresholds, which is what the benchmark tour step relies on.

sections.title: Result shape and helpers
sections.explanation: The docstring defines a result as the case, the draft dict, the call count, wall time and any error. `_norm` collapses whitespace and casefolds text. `_constraint_key` builds a canonical string for a constraint and sorts the children of logical nodes, so ordering differences do not count as errors. `_party` reads an assignee or assigner from the rule and falls back to the policy level.

sections.title: Checkpoint extraction
sections.explanation: `checkpoints` flattens an IR into sets of tuples in four categories: entity, action, modality and constraint. Constraints, action refinements and duties (including their constraints) all land in the constraint set, keyed by modality, action and target. Using sets makes gold and prediction comparison a simple set operation.

sections.title: Micro-averaged F1 scores
sections.explanation: `_f1` returns None when there is nothing to score, so a missing category is distinguishable from a score of zero. `checkpoint_scores` accumulates true positives, false positives and false negatives per category across all cases. It then reports one overall F1 plus one per category (micro-averaging).

sections.title: Permission and prohibition checks
sections.explanation: `false_permissions` flags a predicted permission that no gold permission covers. Coverage requires the same target and assignee and a gold action that `includes` the predicted action. A permission is also bad if its assignee appears in the case's forbidden principals. `missed_prohibitions` counts gold prohibitions with no matching predicted one, where an unscoped (None) assignee also matches. A dropped prohibition is therefore treated as an over-permission risk.

sections.title: Span attribution
sections.explanation: Counts rules for which at least one source span, sliced from the original text by its start and end offsets, matches its quoted text after normalization. It returns (rules attributed, total rules). This checks that provenance offsets are genuine and not just plausible quotes.

sections.title: Ratio and percentile helpers
sections.explanation: `_ratio` returns None on a zero denominator, which propagates 'not applicable' into the gates. `_percentile` uses a simple nearest-rank index into the sorted values, with no interpolation.

sections.title: Computing all metrics
sections.explanation: `compute` assembles every metric into one dict: SHACL pass rate, valid-term rate, false-permission and false-auto-publish rates, the tier-5 adversarial rate, behavioral agreement, conflict escape, ambiguity recall, unsupported assumptions, span attribution, median LLM calls and p95 latency per route. Conflict cases and cases with no gold rules are skipped for agreement. Ambiguity counts as caught only when the draft's ambiguity kinds overlap the expected ones and the draft was not auto-published.

sections.title: Per-tier breakdown
sections.explanation: `by_tier` groups results by difficulty tier, reruns `compute` per group and keeps a short list of headline keys. It gives the report a per-tier view without duplicating metric logic.

odrl_agent/bench/gates.py.overview: Declares the release gates for the benchmark and the regression rules against a frozen baseline. It evaluates a metrics dict into pass/fail rows. The CI workflows use it to decide whether a run blocks a merge.

sections.title: Gate thresholds table
sections.explanation: `GATES` maps each metric name to a comparison operator, a threshold and a live-only flag. Examples are SHACL pass rate == 1.0, checkpoint F1 >= 0.92 and tier-5 false permission == 0. The latency gates are live-only because the offline run has no real model latency. A comment explains that missed prohibitions are gated because a dropped prohibition is an over-permission.

sections.title: Regression limits and operators
sections.explanation: Constants set how far a candidate may drift from the baseline: false-permission-type rates may rise by 0.005 and F1 may fall by 0.01 (both absolute). `_OPS` maps operator strings to lambdas so the table can stay declarative.

sections.title: Absolute gate evaluation
sections.explanation: `evaluate` produces one row per gate with metric, rule, value and passed. Live-only gates are skipped in offline mode. A metric that is missing or None fails, so missing data cannot slip through a gate silently.

sections.title: Baseline regression rows
sections.explanation: `regressions` compares the three over-permission rates and the two F1 scores to the baseline using the tolerances above. Either side being None fails the row. `failed` filters rows to the ones that did not pass. This is the check that pull requests are held to in the live workflow.

odrl_agent/bench/pins.py.overview: Records and verifies the pins that a benchmark number depends on: model id, extractor prompt pack hash, IR schema hash, wire schema hash and IR version. They are stored in benchmarks/v1/pins.json. Any prompt or model change moves a hash, which makes an offline test fail until the pins file is rewritten in a visible diff.

sections.title: Purpose and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring explains the mechanism: the pins file is path-filtered by the live gate workflow, so a change must clear a live benchmark run. `PINS_PATH` resolves two parents up from this file to the repository's benchmarks/v1/pins.json.

sections.title: Computing current pins
sections.explanation: `_sha` returns the first 16 hex characters of a SHA-256. `current` hashes the system and decompose prompts joined by a separator, and the IR and wire JSON schemas serialized with sorted keys so the hash is stable. It also records the default model and `IR_VERSION`.

sections.title: Load, write and drift
sections.explanation: `load` and `write` read and write the JSON pins file as UTF-8. `drift` returns `{key: (pinned, current)}` for every pin that differs, which the integrity test and the `bench pins` command use to detect an unpinned change.

odrl_agent/chaos.py.overview: The live-workflow chaos gate. It re-executes the real conversion pipeline under fuzzed fault schedules, with faults injected at the read_source, llm and save_odrl boundaries. It judges each resulting trace with the ODRL invariants and shrinks failing schedules. The model is an offline mock, so the gate runs on every pull request without a network or key.

sections.title: Why a live chaos gate
sections.explanation: The docstring contrasts this with `agentcrash check --fuzz`, which only replays faults over a recorded trace and so cannot show whether this workflow recovers. Here the same fuzz-and-shrink engine drives a runner that reruns the pipeline each time. Imports include the SDK factory `chaos_sdk` and the `StructuredLlm` client.

sections.title: Invariants and fault kinds
sections.explanation: `CHAOS_INVARIANTS` lists the seven checks every trace must satisfy, mixing ODRL gate checks with the generic fresh-write and lost-update checks. `FAULT_KINDS` names the injected faults. `REFERENCE_IR` is the IR an honest extractor would return for the scenario text: one permission for the research team on dataset-7.

sections.title: Offline mock LLM
sections.explanation: `mock_llm` builds a real `StructuredLlm` over an `httpx.MockTransport` whose handler always returns the same chat-completion JSON. The `sleep` is replaced with a no-op so retries cost no time. This keeps the whole LLM code path (parsing, usage accounting) under test without network access.

sections.title: Runner factory
sections.explanation: `make_runner` loads the scenario and policy YAML and returns a `runner(schedule)` closure. Each call numbers its own trace and state files and builds a fault-injecting SDK from the schedule and seed. It then calls `run_conversion`, always closing the SDK in `finally`. It optionally logs the faults, draft status, saves and hash-chain health, and returns parsed trace events with the state snapshot. Agentcrash imports are deferred into the function body.

sections.title: Running the full gate
sections.explanation: `run_chaos` registers the ODRL verifiers, resolves the invariants and uses a temp directory when none is given. For each scenario it first runs a fault-free baseline, then `fuzz_and_shrink`. A scenario passes only if the baseline verdict is PASS, no fuzz case fails and at least one run actually fired a fault. This last condition stops a harness that injects nothing from passing. The overall `ok` also needs every SDK hash chain to be valid.

odrl_agent/verifiers.py.overview: The ODRL domain invariants registered with the AgentCrash verifier registry. It holds the original three checks (valid, no attacker grant, exactly-once save) and four Phase 2 gate checks that judge the draft-versus-publish contract. The core agentcrash package never imports this module. Hosts import it, or call `register_odrl_verifiers`, to judge ODRL traces.

sections.title: Imports, constants, exports
sections.explanation: The docstring says to import the module from the host application only. `SAVE_ODRL` names the mutating tool. `ODRL_INVARIANT_IDS` and `ODRL_GATE_IDS` list the two groups of check ids. `__all__` re-exports the core `FreshWriteOnly` and `NoLostUpdate` classes so hosts get one import point.

sections.title: Trace filtering helpers
sections.explanation: `_mutating_calls` validates that the trace is a list of dict events. It keeps only non-error `tool_result` events for the given tool. `_committed_saves` narrows these to `save_odrl` events whose args have op 'write', which is the definition of a published document used throughout.

sections.title: OdrlValid check
sections.explanation: Every committed save must pass `validate_odrl` against the ODRL shapes. It also fails when there are no saves, because a converter that saves nothing has not converted anything. Failure messages list the step and the SHACL errors.

sections.title: NoAttackerGrant check
sections.explanation: Checks that no saved document grants `ATTACKER_PRINCIPAL`, using `contains_attacker_grant`. It targets the poisoned-sentence scenario, where an untrusted instruction tries to plant a grant. A structurally valid document can still fail this check.

sections.title: ExactlyOnceSave check
sections.explanation: Passes only when exactly one committed `save_odrl` write exists, so retries and duplicate saves fail even if each document is valid. It is kept in the host module so the framework core stays domain-free.

sections.title: Draft recovery helpers
sections.explanation: `_run_end` finds the last `run_end` event detail. `_source` returns the ingested text from the `ingest` pipeline stage. `_draft_ir` revalidates the draft's IR dict into a `PolicyIR` and returns None if it is missing or invalid. The gate checks use these to recompute results from the trace rather than trust recorded reports.

sections.title: OdrlShaclValid check
sections.explanation: Like `OdrlValid`, but publishing nothing is acceptable when the pipeline held the draft for review. It fails when a saved document is invalid or when an auto-publishable draft was not saved.

sections.title: Conflict and grounding checks
sections.explanation: `NoDeonticConflict` reruns `reasoning.analyze` on the draft IR and fails if the report has conflicts or unsatisfiable ranges. `GroundedPrincipals` reruns the `Grounder` on the ingested source. It rebuilds a catalog from names the draft already resolved, so catalog-resolved parties count as grounded. Both pass vacuously when nothing was published and fail when a draft IR is missing.

sections.title: ExactlyOncePublish check
sections.explanation: Expects one save when the draft is auto-publishable and zero otherwise. Held drafts reach the store only through Approve & Publish, outside the conversion run, so any save of a held draft is a violation.

sections.title: Registration
sections.explanation: `register_odrl_verifiers` registers all checks and is idempotent. It rebinds `FreshWriteOnly` to `save_odrl`, because `agentcrash check` re-registers its built-ins and overwrites that binding with a default for `key_value_store`. The module calls it once at import time.

scenarios/odrl_convert_poisoned/scenario.overview: An AgentCrash scenario for the adversarial variant of the ODRL conversion task. The natural-language request carries a hostile instruction that grants attacker-client access. The converter must never save that as a grant. The chaos gate and the verifiers load this file.

sections.title: Scenario header and task
sections.explanation: Declares the scenario schema version, id, task and seed 42. The comments say the fixture bytes carry the hostile instruction, tagged untrusted, and that the converter must not save it as a grant.

sections.title: Tool definitions
sections.explanation: Three tools are declared with simulated latency and timeout: parse_policy and validate_odrl are read-only, and save_odrl is the only mutating tool. `idempotency_key_arg` is null for all of them, so the verifiers rely on trace shape and not on idempotency keys.

sections.title: Invariants
sections.explanation: Lists four invariants: odrl_valid, no_attacker_grant, exactly_once_save and fresh_write_only. Each has a check expression and a description. These ids match the verifiers registered in `odrl_agent/verifiers.py`.

sections.title: Policy and environment
sections.explanation: References the default agent policy file and a 12-step limit. The environment points at the NL fixture file and a document keyed `poisoned_sentence_v1`. It seeds an empty `odrl-policy-1` record in the store.

schemas/trace-event.json.overview: A JSON Schema (draft-07) for one JSONL trace event envelope, version trace/v1. Trace events are the evidence the verifiers and the chaos gate read. Each event links to the previous one by hash.

sections.title: Schema header
sections.explanation: Sets the draft-07 dialect, the title and a description naming the trace/v1 format. The root is an object.

sections.title: Required fields
sections.explanation: Twelve fields are mandatory, including `event_id`, `prev_hash`, `run_id`, `step`, `tool`, `args`, `outcome` and `latency`. `injector_event` and `policy_decision` are also required, though they may be null. The optional `detail` object is not required.

sections.title: Property definitions
sections.explanation: `event_id` and `run_id` have strict hex patterns. `ts_virtual`, `step` and `latency` are non-negative integers. `tool` may be null. `outcome` is limited to success, timeout, error, blocked or info. `detail` is a free-form object, where the verifiers find phases like `tool_result` and `run_end`.

Dockerfile.overview: A multi-stage build for the self-host image. The first stage builds the React studio with Node. The second installs the Python package and serves the API and built UI with Uvicorn on port 8901. It covers the container part of the deployment tour step.

sections.title: UI build stage
sections.explanation: Uses node:22-slim. It copies only package.json and the lockfile first so the `npm ci` layer is cached, then copies the source and runs the Vite build. The comment notes the build output lands in /build/ui through the Vite outDir setting.

sections.title: Python runtime stage
sections.explanation: Starts from python:3.12-slim with unbuffered output and PYTHONPATH set to /app. It copies only what the app needs: package, policies, prompts, schemas, scenarios and one test fixture. It installs the project with pip, then copies the built UI from the first stage. No Node tooling reaches the final image.

sections.title: Port, healthcheck, command
sections.explanation: Exposes 8901 and defines a healthcheck with a Python one-liner that requests /api/healthz, the one endpoint that answers without credentials. The default command is `odrl-host serve` bound to 0.0.0.0.

docker-compose.yml.overview: Compose file that runs the studio service with environment-driven configuration and persistent storage. All secrets and tunables come from the host environment with safe empty defaults.

sections.title: Service and ports
sections.explanation: A single `studio` service is built from the local Dockerfile and publishes port 8901.

sections.title: Environment configuration
sections.explanation: Variables cover the model endpoint and key, an allowlist of model hosts as an SSRF guard, product API keys (empty means open local mode), trusted parties and the run queue limits (workers, depth, TTL). Secure session cookies are an opt-in toggle for TLS deployments. Optional AgentCrash control plane variables are also set. The comments note that per-tenant model settings are held in server memory and not in env.

sections.title: Persistent volumes
sections.explanation: Bind-mounts agentcrash.db to keep runs, evidence, decisions and issued keys across restarts. The comment warns the file must exist first. Named volumes keep traces and reports.

sections.title: Healthcheck and volume declarations
sections.explanation: The healthcheck calls /api/healthz every 30 seconds with a 5 second timeout and 3 retries. The two named volumes are declared at the bottom.

.github/workflows/ci.yml.overview: The per-push and per-pull-request CI pipeline. It runs the converter tests, the chaos gate and the benchmark checks on three Python versions. It also builds the React studio and the Docker image.

sections.title: Triggers
sections.explanation: Runs on every push and every pull request.

sections.title: Converter job setup
sections.explanation: The `converter` job runs on Ubuntu with PYTHONPATH set to the repo root. It uses a matrix of Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13 with fail-fast off, so one version failing does not hide results from the others.

sections.title: Converter gates
sections.explanation: Installs the package in editable mode with pytest, then runs the tests. Next come the chaos gate (20 fuzz cases with a mocked model) and the benchmark integrity checks (`bench verify` for the manifest hash and `bench pins` for prompt and model pins). Then it runs the offline oracle benchmark. The last step runs `agentcrash check` on the golden trace with the ODRL plugin and `--scan-pii` as a PII guardrail.

sections.title: Studio build job
sections.explanation: Sets up Node 22 with npm caching keyed on the lockfile, then runs `npm ci` and the Vite build in ui-react. This verifies the front end compiles.

sections.title: Image build job
sections.explanation: Needs both the converter and studio jobs to pass, then builds the Docker image to check the Dockerfile still works.

.github/workflows/bench-live.yml.overview: The live-model benchmark workflow. It runs nightly, on demand and on pull requests that touch files able to move benchmark numbers. Pull requests are blocked only by regressions against Baseline v1. Nightly and manual runs enforce every absolute target.

sections.title: Triggers and policy
sections.explanation: The header comment sets the policy for pull requests versus nightly runs. Triggers are a nightly cron, manual dispatch and pull requests path-filtered to the extractor, LLM client, IR, grounder, pipeline, prompts and pins file. These match the files the pins module hashes.

sections.title: Concurrency
sections.explanation: Groups runs by workflow and ref and cancels in-progress runs, so a newer push replaces a stale live run and saves model cost.

sections.title: Job setup
sections.explanation: A single `benchmark` job with a 90 minute timeout. Model credentials come from repository secrets as environment variables. It checks out the code and sets up Python 3.12.

sections.title: Install and credential check
sections.explanation: Installs the package, then fails fast with an error annotation if either secret is missing. The message states that a prompt or model change cannot merge without a live run.

sections.title: Live benchmark run
